Let
\[
f(x)=\frac1{1+tx},\qquad S=2a+1.
\]
The two extremal distributions are:

\[
\nu_{\min}=\frac12\delta_{\frac12-\frac1{2\sqrt S}}
+\frac12\delta_{\frac12+\frac1{2\sqrt S}},
\]
and
\[
\nu_{\max}=\frac1{2S}\delta_0+\frac{S-1}{S}\delta_{1/2}
+\frac1{2S}\delta_1.
\]

Both have the required first three moments. For example, for \(\nu_{\min}\), writing
\[
X=\frac12\pm \frac1{2\sqrt S}
\]
with equal probabilities gives
\[
EX=\frac12,\qquad
EX^2=\frac14+\frac1{4S}=\frac{a+1}{2(2a+1)},
\]
and
\[
EX^3=\frac18+\frac{3}{8S}=\frac{a+2}{4(2a+1)}.
\]
The verification for \(\nu_{\max}\) is immediate from its three atoms.

Now we prove sharpness. Since
\[
f^{(4)}(x)=\frac{24t^4}{(1+tx)^5}>0,
\]
Hermite interpolation gives useful one-sided cubic bounds.

For the two interior nodes
\[
u=\frac12-\frac1{2\sqrt S},\qquad v=\frac12+\frac1{2\sqrt S},
\]
let \(P\) be the cubic Hermite interpolant satisfying
\[
P(u)=f(u),\quad P'(u)=f'(u),\quad P(v)=f(v),\quad P'(v)=f'(v).
\]
The Hermite remainder is
\[
f(x)-P(x)=\frac{f^{(4)}(\xi)}{4!}(x-u)^2(x-v)^2\ge 0,
\]
so \(P\le f\) on \([0,1]\). Since every admissible \(X\) has the same first three moments,
\[
Ef(X)\ge EP(X)=\int P\,d\nu_{\min}=\int f\,d\nu_{\min}.
\]
Thus \(\nu_{\min}\) attains the infimum.

Similarly, let \(Q\) be the cubic Hermite interpolant satisfying
\[
Q(0)=f(0),\quad Q(1/2)=f(1/2),\quad Q'(1/2)=f'(1/2),\quad Q(1)=f(1).
\]
Then
\[
f(x)-Q(x)=\frac{f^{(4)}(\xi)}{4!}x\left(x-\frac12\right)^2(x-1)\le 0
\]
on \([0,1]\), so \(Q\ge f\). Hence
\[
Ef(X)\le EQ(X)=\int Q\,d\nu_{\max}=\int f\,d\nu_{\max},
\]
and \(\nu_{\max}\) attains the supremum.

Compute the two values:
\[
\inf E\frac1{1+tX}
=
\frac{1+t/2}{(1+t/2)^2-\frac{t^2}{4S}},
\]
and
\[
\sup E\frac1{1+tX}
=
\frac{t^2+4St+4S}{2S(1+t)(2+t)}.
\]
Subtracting gives
\[
\Delta_a(t)
=
\frac{(S-1)t^4}{2S(1+t)(2+t)\big((S-1)t^2+4St+4S\big)}.
\]
Since \(S=2a+1\), this is

\[
\boxed{
\Delta_a(t)=
\frac{a t^4}{(2a+1)(1+t)(2+t)\left(2a t^2+4(2a+1)t+4(2a+1)\right)}
}.
\]
